title: Roadmap 9: web framework operations
seriesDescription: Topic-by-topic quizzes that follow the backend interview roadmap: language core, concurrency, DSA habits, web frameworks, data access, databases, messaging, resilience, security, testing, system design, and LLM/agent engineering.
description: Async and streaming endpoints, pagination and idempotency, API versioning, GraphQL N+1, config and secrets, scheduled jobs across instances, and liveness versus readiness.
source: Interview roadmap study plan (Java/Spring Boot and Python/FastAPI)

questions.prompt: A FastAPI endpoint is declared `async def` and calls `requests.get(url)` (a blocking HTTP client) inside it. What is the effect under load?

options.text: It blocks the event loop while waiting, so other requests on that worker stall.
options.why: Right: async def runs on the event loop and a blocking call freezes it.

options.text: FastAPI automatically moves the body to a worker thread pool, so only this one request waits.
options.why: That is done for plain def endpoints, not for async def ones.

options.text: The call raises an error because blocking calls are banned there.
options.why: Nothing forbids it; it just runs and quietly hurts throughput.

options.text: Only this request slows down, since each request has its own loop.
options.why: Workers share one event loop across requests; that is the problem.

questions.explanation: Use an async client such as httpx.AsyncClient inside async def, or declare the endpoint with plain def so FastAPI runs it in a thread pool. Same idea in Spring WebFlux: never block a Netty event-loop thread.

questions.prompt: A Spring Boot service needs a production database password. What is the sound way to supply it?

options.text: Read it from an environment variable or secret store, bound to a property placeholder.
options.why: Right: config stays outside the artifact and differs per environment.

options.text: Commit it in application-prod.yml, since that profile only loads when running in production.
options.why: A profile selects a file; it does not hide a secret in version control.

options.text: Give the @Value field a hard-coded default so local runs work.
options.why: A default in code ships the secret in every build and log of the class.

options.text: Base64-encode it in application.properties so it is not readable.
options.why: Base64 is an encoding, not encryption; anyone can reverse it.

questions.explanation: Spring maps env vars such as SPRING_DATASOURCE_PASSWORD onto properties, and @ConfigurationProperties binds them into typed beans. In Python, pydantic-settings does the same: a BaseSettings class reads env vars (and .env files) and validates them at startup.

questions.prompt: Select all that apply. Why is keyset (cursor) pagination often preferred over OFFSET for a large, frequently updated feed?

options.text: OFFSET n must walk past and discard n rows, so deep pages get slower.
options.why: True: cost grows with the offset.

options.text: Inserts between page requests can make OFFSET repeat or skip rows.
options.why: True: the window shifts when rows are added or removed.

options.text: A cursor on an indexed, unique sort key such as (created_at, id) seeks straight to the next page.
options.why: True: WHERE (created_at, id) < (?, ?) ORDER BY ... LIMIT uses the index.

options.text: Cursors let a client jump directly to page 500.
options.why: False: cursors only move forward or back from a known position.

options.text: Cursors work even if the sort column has duplicates and no tiebreaker.
options.why: False: without a unique tiebreaker, rows can be skipped or repeated.

questions.explanation: Offset is fine for small, stable lists and when random page access matters. For feeds and infinite scroll use an opaque cursor encoding the last (sort key, id).

questions.prompt: A client times out calling POST /payments and retries. Which server design stops the customer being charged twice?

options.text: Store the Idempotency-Key with its outcome under a unique constraint and replay the saved response.
options.why: Right: a retry with the same key returns the first result.

options.text: Reject any payment with the same amount and user inside a 60 second window.
options.why: A heuristic; it blocks legitimate repeat purchases and misses slow retries.

options.text: Switch the endpoint to GET so that intermediaries can retry safely.
options.why: GET must be safe and side-effect free; a charge is not.

options.text: Tell clients never to retry and treat timeouts as failures.
options.why: The charge may have succeeded; telling clients to give up loses that state.

questions.explanation: The key is client-generated (usually a UUID). Insert it first, run the charge once, save the response; concurrent duplicates hit the unique constraint. Also store a request fingerprint and reject the same key with a different body.

questions.prompt: True or false: adding a new optional field to a JSON response is normally a backward-compatible change for existing clients.

options.text: True
options.why: Right: well-behaved clients ignore unknown fields.

options.text: False
options.why: Adding an optional field is the standard non-breaking change.

questions.explanation: Removing or renaming a field, changing a type, or making an optional request field required are the breaking changes that need a new version or a deprecation window. Tolerant-reader clients are the assumption.

questions.prompt: A GraphQL query fetches 50 posts and each post's author. Logs show 1 query for posts and 50 separate queries for authors. What is the standard fix?

options.text: Use a DataLoader that batches author ids per tick into one WHERE id IN query.
options.why: Right: the 50 lookups collapse into one batched query.

options.text: Put an HTTP cache in front of the single /graphql endpoint so repeated author lookups are served from cache.
options.why: POST bodies differ per query, and a cache does not remove the N lookups.

options.text: Limit the query depth to one so authors cannot be nested.
options.why: That removes a legitimate feature without fixing the lookup pattern.

options.text: Replace the posts query with OFFSET pagination.
options.why: Pagination changes the list size, not the per-item author lookups.

questions.explanation: Resolvers run per field, so a naive author resolver issues one query per post. DataLoader (graphql-java's DataLoader, Strawberry's DataLoader) batches and caches per request.

questions.prompt: A Spring Boot app runs on three instances behind a load balancer, with `@Scheduled(cron = "0 0 2 * * *")` sending nightly invoices. Select all statements that are true.

options.text: Without coordination, every instance runs the job, so invoices can go out three times.
options.why: True: @Scheduled is per JVM.

options.text: A lock such as ShedLock or a dedicated scheduler instance makes the run happen once.
options.why: True: you must add coordination yourself.

options.text: If all instances are down at 02:00, the run is skipped and not replayed on restart.
options.why: True: cron triggers are not persisted or caught up.

options.text: Spring elects one instance to run it, using the shared database.
options.why: False: it has no built-in cluster awareness.

options.text: Spring stores missed executions and replays them after a restart.
options.why: False: that needs a persistent scheduler such as Quartz.

questions.explanation: Make jobs idempotent as well, since locks can fail. Same pattern in Python: APScheduler in each worker runs per process, FastAPI BackgroundTasks die with the process, and Celery beat must run as exactly one scheduler.

questions.prompt: True or false: a Kubernetes liveness probe should check the database, so pods restart when the database is down.

options.text: True
options.why: Restarting pods does not repair a database outage.

options.text: False
options.why: Right: liveness should only report that the process is stuck.

questions.explanation: Liveness failing triggers a restart, so tying it to a dependency can cause a restart storm. Put dependency checks in readiness, which only removes the pod from load balancing. Actuator exposes /actuator/health/liveness and /actuator/health/readiness.
